#5497. Amazon plans its first large-scale data centers in Washington state as residents raise concerns

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:36 am

Amazon is moving toward building its first large-scale data centers in Washington state, with a proposed campus in Walla Walla County and a second in the Tri-Cities that the company confirmed this week.

The expansion into Amazon’s home state comes amid nationwide pushback against the rapid deployment of new AI data centers. Tuesday’s election underscored the scrutiny facing data center developers, with voters in communities across several states backing limits on new projects. In Eastern Washington, the Amazon proposals have drawn calls for greater environmental oversight and a temporary halt to data center development.

Amazon already has a substantial footprint in neighboring Oregon, where industry tracker Baxtel lists 64 AWS data center sites. Expansion there has divided communities, with residents pushing for restrictions over power and water concerns while some Eastern Oregon officials warn that slowing development would jeopardize jobs and tax revenue.

Both proposed Washington campuses would initially include three data center buildings. The Walla Walla County site covers roughly 134 acres in Wallula Gap, while the Tri-Cities campus is on a 1,000 acre property in the city of West Richland and could eventually grow to 21 buildings. The company is already operating smaller data centers in the state, including Seattle.

The Tri-City Herald first reported Monday that Amazon was behind the West Richland project. The company plans to hold a community open house Nov. 19 to discuss the proposal.

A full build-out of the West Richland campus could create more than 1,000 full-time data center jobs, Amazon said. Dallas real estate firm Trammell Crow initially purchased the property from the estate of agricultural businessman Frank Tiegs, who died in 2024, before selling it to Amazon.

Nearby residents have raised concerns about the planned campus, in part because of its proximity to about 200 homes. Residents asked the local city council to approve a temporary moratorium, but at a meeting Tuesday evening, council members adopted rules that removed a data center noise exemption, banned them in light industrial zones, and prohibited cryptocurrency mining. The council failed to pass a moratorium, NonStop Local reported.

Amazon says the upcoming open house will give residents an opportunity to ask questions about the planned development. A spokesperson described a “science fair” format, with booths hosted by experts discussing water and energy usage, job creation, noise and environmental impacts.

“We’re committed to growing responsibly and we want the community to leave the Open House with a better understanding of this project and what it could mean for the area,” the spokesperson said via email.

At Wallula Gap, a recent public-comment period offers an indication of the scrutiny Amazon faces.

Of the 706 submissions received during a 30-day comment period that closed Oct. 12, only 23 — about 3% — supported the project, according to an analysis by the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin. Most of the supportive comments came from the area, and many predicated their support on more stringent oversight of the proposed facility near the Columbia River.

More than 500 submissions came from outside Walla Walla County, according to the Union-Bulletin. Many included template language calling for an Environmental Impact Statement — a higher level of environmental assessment than currently required for the campus.

The proposed facility is located at the Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. The three proposed single-story data center buildings would create approximately 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

The land is zoned for “industrial agriculture – mixed” applications, which the company said includes data centers. Amazon’s involvement in the project was first reported by the Tri-City Herald in February.

Amazon’s FAQs for the two sites address several issues raised by residents, including electricity costs and water use.

Rising electric bills nationwide and the climate impacts of new gas power plants and backup diesel generators have made energy use a top concern. Amazon said it will work with local utilities and other officials “to ensure that our data centers do not raise electricity bills for people in our communities.”

The company reports that it matched all electricity consumed across its global operations with renewable energy sources in 2023 and 2024. That annual, company-wide accounting measure does not mean each facility runs on renewable electricity around the clock.

Amazon also points to its investment of “billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects,” including a proposed small modular reactor plant near the Tri-Cities that could come online in the 2030s.

“This project will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said in its FAQ.

Amid concerns about water shortages, Amazon touts water-use rates that it says beat other tech companies and are much lower than irrigated farming. Those rates, however, do not include water used in electricity generation. Many power plants use water to produce steam that drives electricity-generating turbines and for cooling, with some water lost through evaporation.

At both locations, Amazon says it will pay 100% of its property taxes rather than seek tax breaks for building in the communities. The company says its taxes are higher than most industrial uses and directly support schools, roads, fire and police, and other services.

Beyond addressing concerns about its data centers, Amazon is making a broader case for why communities should welcome them. Last month, the company launched its Built Together initiative, committing more than $1 billion in additional investments over five years to U.S. communities where it operates data centers. The funding supports efforts including free community college, energy upgrades for homes and buildings, and workforce training.

In announcing the program, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman framed data center development as part of a global race for AI dominance. He warned that local and state moratoriums could harm the U.S. economy and national security.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman said. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

In West Richland, residents will have an opportunity to question Amazon’s plans — and the assurances accompanying them — at the company’s upcoming open house.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/5 to note that Amazon is operating smaller-scale data centers in Washington, but not campuses of the scope being proposed in Eastern Washington.

#5496. Their Kids Loved The Little Gym. Then They Saw a $20 Million Franchise Opportunity.

Griffin Gordon and Kevin Condon were The Little Gym customers before they became franchise investors. Now they own 30 gyms.

Before Griffin Gordon and Kevin Condon owned dozens of The Little Gym locations, they were parents watching their children enjoy gymnastics classes at the franchise. Their kids were tumbling, running and leaving class asking to do it all again.

As a customer, Gordon was impressed that The Little Gym staff members knew the children’s names, greeted their parents and made families feel welcome.

Gordon and Condon had met years earlier at the University of Chicago’s Booth School of Business before pursuing different careers. Condon became a co-founder of Hidden River Strategic Capital, a Philadelphia-based private equity firm that invests in small businesses. Gordon split his career between private equity investing and running small and midsize companies, later founding an investment firm focused on franchisees.

Their paths converged around an opportunity involving Richard Moore, a longtime Little Gym operator whose family had spent nearly three decades building the business. Moore wanted to keep growing. His parents were ready to retire. An advisor introduced him to Gordon and Condon, who saw a chance to pair an experienced operator with the capital and support to expand.

In 2023, Gordon and Condon’s firms invested in seven North Carolina locations of The Little Gym, forming the foundation of a business called Somersault. Three years later, the partners say their footprint has grown to more than 30 locations, with another 10-plus in development. Their business generates nearly $20 million in revenue.

They credit that expansion to a combination of familiar ingredients, including an established brand. Here’s why they decided to invest in The Little Gym and open new franchise locations.

The following interview has been lightly edited for clarity and concision.

Why invest so aggressively, growing from seven locations to more than 30?Kevin Condon: Ultimately, we’re backing management teams and organizational leaders. We have a really good team here, which has allowed us to scale at this pace and given us the conviction to continue putting money behind the business.

The other piece is the repeatable process in franchising. You acquire a business or open a location, and you have a playbook. With a good team and good operators, you can repeat that playbook. We’ve taken a strong brand and expanded through acquisitions and new openings.

Griffin Gordon: Kevin’s firm has done a lot of franchisee investing. My firm focuses solely on it. The Little Gym has the things we find attractive: a growing market of parents who want high-quality services for their kids, a strong brand and attractive unit economics when the business is operated well.

What else made this particular opportunity attractive?Gordon: In our view, The Little Gym is the best brand serving its target age range. There are imitators, but we don’t think they match the quality of its curriculum and operating playbook.

We also have a strong franchisor partner in Unleashed Brands. To invest in franchisees, you need a partnership approach and confidence that the franchisor values that relationship, too.

How did those factors turn into an actual investment?Gordon: It was equal parts purposeful and opportunistic. We were interested in franchisee investing because of its repeatability and scalability. We were also focused on child enrichment because we thought it was an attractive market if you did things right.

How much did being customers influence your decision to start locations of your own?Condon: We only have so much time and money to allocate. The Little Gym offered the opportunity to invest in what we consider a category leader in youth enrichment, particularly children’s recreational gymnastics and related activities.

The system has been around for 50 years. This year was its 50th anniversary, which was a major milestone for the franchise.

There’s an established playbook, and both our business and the overall system are growing. When you have a strong brand and the unit economics to open a location, ramp it up and become profitable, you can create returns for investors, jobs for employees and outcomes for families. That makes it easy to understand why we want to continue investing our time and money.

What are the most important elements of that repeatable playbook?Gordon: There are two sides to it: the fundamentals that don’t change, and the opportunity to modernize the business for today’s parents and children. The fundamentals include building and investing in a great team, genuinely caring about the curriculum and developing authentic connections with the communities where you operate.

How do those fundamentals connect with changes to the business?Gordon: You also have to work with the franchisor to make sure the curriculum supports the outcomes everyone wants: Confident, self-assured, well-adjusted children who have an opportunity to become physically active early in life.

That dovetails with Unleashed Brands’ investments in infrastructure. Before our investment, The Little Gym didn’t have much in the way of technology, systems and infrastructure. It operated more like a small-business-owned enterprise.

Since Unleashed Brands’ acquisition, we’ve been able to combine the traditional strengths of the business with improvements in the technology we use to operate it and the systems customers interact with.

There’s also been a more thoughtful approach to customer acquisition and marketing, alongside continued investment in the programming. The offering has to remain competitive with parents’ changing demands and schedules.

Condon: The core curriculum is the secret sauce. It’s been part of what has made The Little Gym special for 50 years. But you can build on that. For example, Unleashed introduced an app this year to help parents engage with their children’s classes and see milestones and pictures.

That’s something that obviously didn’t exist 50 years ago. It connects what The Little Gym has historically done well with what a modern parent wants from a class.

Both of you have children who attended. What were their experiences like?Condon: Smiles from ear to ear. They’d spend 45 to 60 minutes in class, come out sweaty and exhausted, and their first question would be, “Can we do that again?”

There’s a joy in watching children move and take appropriate risks, whether they’re learning a cartwheel or somersault, jumping, running, singing, following directions or engaging with other kids.

Much of what I’m describing is in that 2-to-6-year-old age range, although we serve younger and older children, too. I saw it with my own kids, and we see it across the children coming through our locations. There’s a consistency to that experience. It’s unadulterated childhood joy.

Why franchise instead of starting an independent business?Condon: In small business, the opportunity to be part of something with a name as established as The Little Gym is attractive. We invest in both franchised and non-franchised businesses. One benefit of franchising is that you can be part of something much bigger than you could create on your own.

If we started a competitor, we wouldn’t have 50 years of history or an established brand. Franchising gives us an affiliation with a much larger organization and system.

You pay royalties and operate within certain rules. But in this case, we believe the playbook and brand provide more benefits than going it alone.

Gordon: When done correctly, franchising should be like buying a small business with the benefit of a national platform. Those two things should work together. That’s what we believe we have with The Little Gym.

What should someone do if they’re interested in franchising but don’t know where to start?Gordon: One of the best things about franchising is the availability of information. Not every detail is public, but the information you need to understand the model is there.

In particular, there’s a list of franchisees in the back of the franchise disclosure document. If you’re evaluating a system, start calling owners and learning from them. These are people who have already done what you’re trying to do. I can’t think of a better resource.

Condon: Find something you’re passionate about, particularly if you’ll be the operator. Even if you won’t operate the business yourself, you still need to care about it. In our case, as investors helping build and scale a company, we also need an operator who knows how to execute the playbook successfully.

What lesson have you learned while building the company?Gordon: The lesson we’ve learned and continue to learn is that this business is all about people. People sometimes hear about The Little Gym and think it sounds simple. It’s a simple business to understand, but a challenging business to operate well.

The business depends on our ability to find the best people, train them effectively and give them career opportunities. That might mean moving beyond a teaching role, taking on more responsibility within a gym or eventually overseeing multiple locations.

What milestones are you working toward? Could revenue eventually reach $100 million?Condon: That sounds great.

Gordon: We’ve gone from seven locations to more than 30 in three years. We’ve quadrupled our footprint. Doing that again over the next couple of years would be aggressive, but we’re big believers in the brand and our business, and we want to keep growing.

#5495. Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 5, 2026 at 2:27 pm

Google is giving Seattle’s Allen Institute for AI about $5 million in funding, plus another $1.8 million in cloud credits, to turn an AI weather model developed by Google Research into a tool for projecting climate change decades into the future.

The money will help Ai2 build an open-source model designed to give scientists, water agencies and other planners a faster, more accurate look at how rainfall, temperatures and water supplies could change over the next five to 50 years.

Announced Wednesday morning, the three-year project pairs funding from Google.org, the company’s philanthropic arm, with technical support from Google Research. Ai2 will add four people to its eight-person climate modeling team to do the work.

Google’s work on the model centers on weather, looking ahead a year at most. It has less interest and expertise in climate projections that run decades into the future, said Oliver Watt-Meyer, Ai2’s director of research for AI climate modeling.

“Climate modeling is a bit more of a public good,” he said. “It is information that people need to know, but it’s often more government agencies that are thinking about this.”

Starting with Google’s model: Ai2’s model, NeuralGCM+, will build on Google’s NeuralGCM, which mixes traditional physics equations with AI. Watt-Meyer, who wrote about NeuralGCM for the journal Nature when Google published its research in 2024, said the model does well at forecasting weather and at recreating past climate.

In that piece, he also pointed out its limits: some of its long runs broke down, and when researchers simulated ocean temperatures about 7 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than today, its predictions for the atmosphere didn’t make physical sense.

Under the new project, Ai2 will try to fix both problems. It will connect NeuralGCM+ to an ocean and sea ice model, with the goal of running stable simulations that span decades. It will also build more established physics into the model, then check its predictions for a warmer world against results from traditional climate models.

Ai2’s climate team is made up largely of atmospheric scientists, with the engineers and computing power of an AI institute behind them.

Ai2 is “uniquely positioned to extend Google’s NeuralGCM model into the next generation of long-term climate projections,” said Alex Diaz, head of applied science at Google.org, in a statement, citing the institute’s climate science expertise and commitment to open research.

Where the idea started: The team’s origins go back to the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, who took an interest in climate modeling before his death in 2018. His company, then known as Vulcan, launched the climate modeling project in 2019, and the group moved to Ai2 in 2021. Allen had founded the nonprofit AI institute in 2014.

The original plan was to combine physics and AI. The group set that aside because the AI couldn’t be trained well inside older climate models written in Fortran, a decades-old programming language. Google wrote NeuralGCM in modern code that solves that problem.

In that way, Watt-Meyer said, “This is actually kind of coming full circle for us.”

Ai2 already has its own family of AI climate models, called the Ai2 Climate Emulator, or ACE. These models rely entirely on AI and run much faster than NeuralGCM. But versions trained only on historical data struggle to project a climate the planet hasn’t experienced yet.

Watt-Meyer said NeuralGCM’s design could hold up better as the world warms, because the laws of physics built into it won’t change.

The timeline: The first step is releasing the code for training NeuralGCM, which has been tied to Google’s internal systems. Making it public will let other researchers train their own versions, including on common GPUs rather than only Google’s own chips. Ai2 expects to release it within the first year, with work on the ocean model running in parallel.

Making the model reliable in a warmer world is the hardest part, and it could take longer than three years. “We don’t know if it’ll work necessarily,” Watt-Meyer said.

He said AI coding agents are changing what his team thinks it can get done in that time. The tools are well suited to translating old code into modern programming languages. In one case, an outside group converted a well-known ocean model from Fortran into the same language NeuralGCM uses, so Ai2 won’t have to build its own.

Watt-Meyer called the tools “a real game changer” for simulation. “It’s kind of a golden era for this kind of scientific computing,” he said.

Google Research will keep developing NeuralGCM for forecasts of a few weeks to a year, and the two teams will share training code and data. One of Google’s lead NeuralGCM researchers is spending three days at Ai2 this week.

Who would use the model: Watt-Meyer pointed to questions such as how rainfall could change in the Southwest, a key issue for water planning around Lake Powell on the Colorado River. Insurance and reinsurance companies already use Ai2’s ACE models in their research.

Asked whether data center developers could use these kinds of models, Watt-Meyer said they could help answer questions about cooling, access to renewable energy and risks such as extreme weather and rising seas. But it isn’t clear if the industry is paying attention.

“There’s so much frantic energy to build these things as fast as possible,” he said. “I’m not sure people are really seriously considering this kind of climate data, though maybe they should be a bit more.”

Correction: An earlier version of this story gave an incorrect date for the start of the climate modeling effort at Vulcan. It started in 2019.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5494. First X-BAT fighter jet prototype unveiled as Shield AI preps Seattle area factory for 2027 launch

by John Cook on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:26 amNovember 4, 2026 at 8:41 am

Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle.

Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas.

The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s.

In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing.

The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire.

“This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post. “That is no small feat.”

San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September.

It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare.

“The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.”

The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways.

“Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million.

Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year.

With the prototype built, Shield AI’s engineering team is focusing on proving out its vertical-takeoff-and-landing mechanics in Kansas ahead of initial flight trials later this year.

Harris detailed a multi-phase testing campaign ahead:

“We’ve built the first aircraft,” Harris wrote. “Now it’s time to go prove what it can do.”

#5493. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5491. Washington voters keep millionaires tax, splitting tech leaders over the state’s competitive edge

by Todd Bishop, Lisa Stiffler & Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 10:10 amNovember 4, 2026 at 10:18 am

Washington voters appear to have upheld the state’s new tax on high earners, putting the state on track to lose its place among the nine states without an income tax — a status that tech leaders have long touted as an edge in recruiting companies and talent.

Initiative 645, which would repeal the 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, was trailing 58% to 42% in election-night returns. King County voters rejected the repeal by an even wider margin, with 66.5% voting no. The repeal would need about 62% of the remaining ballots to pass, according to a Seattle Times estimate.

The tax has divided the Seattle tech community since lawmakers unveiled the proposal in February. Some founders and investors warned it would drive talent and capital out of the state, while others called those fears overblown.

Madrona, the Seattle venture capital firm, gave $250,000 to the repeal campaign, making it one of the biggest donors.

“The outcome on the income tax should be disappointing for all Washingtonians as having no income tax was a major source of competitive advantage for the state,” said Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director, responding to questions from GeekWire.

McIlwain, who urged voters to repeal the tax in a GeekWire op-ed in October, said the state saw record economic growth and job creation after voters rejected an income tax in 2010. “I am concerned for the future ability of Washington state to be competitive,” he wrote.

Ben Golden, an attorney and advisor to Pacific Northwest startups and investors, countered that the election outcome demonstrates “that Washingtonians are ready to invest in ourselves.”

“There’s lots of hard work to follow to ensure that revenue is spent wisely, but at least (Washington) will be ready for the wave of Medicaid cuts and AI job disruption on the horizon,” added Golden, who in February penned an op-ed in support of the tax.

And while some residents will leave for tax havens, Golden said, “the opportunity remains ripe for the investor community and startups to build and grow in this healthy and talent-packed region.”

Brian Fioca, a Seattle-based serial entrepreneur and investor, hopes the additional tax dollars will improve the quality of life in the state overall.

“Washington is a wonderful place to live and build a company, full of extraordinary people and talent,” said Fioca, who also offered an earlier op-ed on the issue. “If someone decides not to start a business here, or chooses to leave because of this tax, that’s not someone I’d be particularly excited to work with or invest in anyway.”

Asked whether the outcome changes how Madrona thinks about investing in Washington, McIlwain didn’t address the state specifically. “Our goal remains to find and partner with amazing founders and their teams to build enduring companies that create innovative products, jobs and economic returns,” he said.

State Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, was an original architect of the tax and the prime sponsor of the bill that created it. As Senate majority leader, he kept reworking the measure to win votes until the final days of this year’s legislative session. Pedersen, who has been in the Legislature since 2007, is also executive vice president and general counsel at Seattle construction and engineering firm McKinstry.

At the No on 645 campaign’s election-night event in Seattle on Tuesday, Pedersen celebrated the outcome.

“We have been saddled with an anchor around our neck, with a tax system that is bad for working people, that’s bad for small businesses, that’s bad for just about everybody except for the one percent,” he said, as seen in a video posted on Instagram.

The No on 645 campaign touted a coalition of working families, labor unions, teachers, small business owners and others — and attracted endorsements from state celebrities like Rick Steves, the Edmonds-based travel writer, and “Jeopardy!” host Ken Jennings.

The tax applies only to income above the $1 million threshold, so a household earning $1.5 million would owe $49,500. It takes effect on 2028 income, with the first payments due in April 2029.

Jeff Bezos, Howard Schultz and Rich Barton have all moved out of state in recent years, though each described the move in personal terms.

McIlwain, who moved with his family from Georgia to Seattle 26 years ago, became a Georgia resident again two years ago. That was before lawmakers unveiled the millionaires tax in February.

In 2010, Steve Ballmer and Microsoft helped fund the campaign that defeated a statewide income tax, but the region’s biggest tech companies stayed out of this fight. The state projects the tax will raise $3 billion to $4 billion a year from roughly 25,000 households. Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it into law in March, along with tax breaks for small businesses and lower-income families.

A lawsuit filed in April by former Attorney General Rob McKenna and former state Supreme Court Justice Phil Talmadge argues the tax is unconstitutional, citing a 1933 ruling that classified income as property, which the state constitution says must be taxed at a uniform rate.

The case will likely go to the state Supreme Court, where Democrat-backed candidates led four of five races on Tuesday’s ballot as of election-night returns, according to the Washington State Standard.

#5490. Everyone Has AI Now. Your Next Competitive Advantage Is the People You’re Ignoring.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is no longer a differentiator in the workplace. Human computing power (in collaboration with AI) is the new focus.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Everyone is in an unavoidable race to develop, deploy and integrate AI solutions that give their business operations an edge. The difficulty, at this point, is that AI is available to everyone. Yes, one person can use it more efficiently than the next, but as a new generation of AI-native workers enters the workforce, the “we use AI better than the next guy” advantage is shrinking.

Thoughtful leaders should be using AI, but while it can automate tasks, it can’t eliminate distractions, improve conversations or change how people experience the spaces where they work. As this new digital transformation charges ahead, many teams are overlooking the physical environments that quietly shape their human performance each day.

When you step back, it’s easy to see that AI adoption is no longer the game-changing factor it once was. Instead, workplace design is the next competitive differentiator that will help human teams amplify their AI outputs the best.

AI has many functions and the list of its capabilities is growing all the time. It’s hyper-efficient. It’s good at synthesizing data. It’s cost-effective and can scale without much trouble.

But it is still software. It’s controlled by algorithms. It’s trapped in a machine (even the “Cloud” has to run off physical data centers). That means it can’t address many of the physical human needs in the workplace like when it comes to how people operate and collaborate.

As AI advances, the computing power of the human brain is the part of the equation that is starting to become a deciding factor. The speed (or lack thereof) at which humans can use AI can quickly become a limiting factor in its impact.

The struggle is that it isn’t digital computing power but physical environments that have the most influence on cognitive performance. For instance, Harvard School of Public Health found that simple things like better indoor air quality can affect cognition and, by extension, productivity.

Something like office air pollution isn’t a factor that Claude can compute, or Gemini can jerry-rig. It requires physical solutions and a human mind to design, create and deploy.

It’s important to shift mindsets here when it comes to office environments. Buying that air purifier, for example, isn’t just a health benefit carried over from the past few years of safe distancing. It’s a chance to improve the thinking and performance of your team.

That’s your first step. Stop seeing basic office environmental things like better lighting or cleaner air and water as fundamental requirements. Look at them as investments that give you an edge.

It’s essential that leaders realize how the advantages are shifting. Three years ago, using AI when a competitor wasn’t doing so was a clear advantage. Now, everyone has AI, but those with the best human work environments have the best chance at creating a synergistic advantage through the combination of their machine and human elements.

Investing in overlooked competitive advantages like clean air, low sound, better lighting and other workplace design elements can help:

All of these are more than employee benefits. They are competitive advantages that increase performance through environments that are not just AI-powered but are also human-aligned.

The key is finding ways to incorporate human advantages in a workspace that are as low-lift as possible. Take sound as an example. How loud or “noisy” a space is will impact people’s concentration. What makes a space “noisy” is something called reverberation time, explains RPG Acoustical System, which is the amount of time it takes for sound waves to get below certain decibels. The longer it takes, the noisier a room sounds.

Leaders can take this into consideration when designing or arranging workspaces. They can make sound waves decrease more quickly through the use of sound-absorbing elements, such as rugs or fabrics hung on the wall, wood furniture pieces and drop ceilings.

AI in the workplace is about more than productivity. Artificial intelligence is hyper-productive in a way that humans are just starting to comprehend. It can produce at such a prodigious level that, in most areas of work, the need to have more output won’t be the problem moving forward.

Instead, employers should be designing workplaces that support better work. As machines crank up the output in nearly every work environment, the offices with the highest-performing human workers will have the best chance of producing the highest-quality work. This makes optimizing human cognition and collaboration a priority.

It is an advantage that few leaders are thinking about as everyone races to invest more in the latest AI solutions. Don’t stop investing in AI, but start thinking about your human workers again, too. Investing in overlooked areas like workplace design can be the quiet way to give yourself an advantage in the AI/human world that is unfolding.

Everyone is in an unavoidable race to develop, deploy and integrate AI solutions that give their business operations an edge. The difficulty, at this point, is that AI is available to everyone. Yes, one person can use it more efficiently than the next, but as a new generation of AI-native workers enters the workforce, the “we use AI better than the next guy” advantage is shrinking.

Thoughtful leaders should be using AI, but while it can automate tasks, it can’t eliminate distractions, improve conversations or change how people experience the spaces where they work. As this new digital transformation charges ahead, many teams are overlooking the physical environments that quietly shape their human performance each day.

When you step back, it’s easy to see that AI adoption is no longer the game-changing factor it once was. Instead, workplace design is the next competitive differentiator that will help human teams amplify their AI outputs the best.

#5489. I Built My Identity Around My Career, Then Illness Took It Away. Here’s What I Learned About Purpose.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

A title can disappear overnight, but the skills beneath it don’t. Three questions to identify the strengths that carry over to whatever comes next.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I nearly passed out at work before I admitted something was wrong. It wasn’t that I didn’t recognize my symptoms were serious. It was that leaving my career felt more dangerous than the health problems I was struggling with.

That’s the part of the story I used to leave out, because it was the hardest to admit: My body was telling me to stop, and I kept ignoring it because I had built my whole identity around being unstoppable and around my role as an occupational therapist (OT). I had studied and trained extensively to become a licensed OT. I had formed close friendships with colleagues. I relied on the income. And I quietly believed that being an OT was what made me valuable. Eventually, my health declined further, and the decision I couldn’t make was made for me: I was forced to retire due to illness.

At first, I grieved what was. I felt anxious about the sudden change in our family’s finances, the disruption to our routines, and the loss of my identity without the title of “occupational therapist.” I expected those feelings. What I didn’t expect was relief.

That relief unsettled me more than my diagnoses had. If working as an OT was truly my purpose, why did losing it feel like setting something down? Why did I feel a new sense of freedom? I had spent years telling patients that their identity was bigger than any one role. It turns out I didn’t truly believe that about myself until I had no choice.

I believe most professionals and entrepreneurs confuse occupation with purpose because a career gives us something purpose alone cannot: proof. A job title is proof. A paycheck is proof. Purpose isn’t. You can’t list meaning on a résumé, so we let what’s measurable stand in for what isn’t. The longer we stay in a role, the more our routines, relationships and self-worth revolve around it, until it becomes hard to tell the difference between what we do and who we are.

That isn’t a character flaw. It’s a rational response to how most workplaces operate. Advancement is rewarded; questioning the path is not. So reflection gets postponed until something forces it: an illness, a layoff, a restructuring, a loss, a change in a relationship. And when the question of purpose finally arrives, it rarely feels like curiosity. It feels like a crisis.

Here’s what no one told me: Rebuilding doesn’t start with finding a new purpose. It starts with figuring out which parts of your identity are genuinely yours and which were borrowed from your job. Telling the two apart takes longer than most people expect, because a role can borrow your voice without you noticing.

I rebuilt by looking for what stayed constant across every version of my work, before, during and after my time as an OT. A few things stood out. I could explain complicated things simply. I was drawn to helping people understand their situations better than they had before. And I was always energized by connection rather than credentials. Those traits showed up whether I was working in a clinic, writing a food blog or speaking on camera. My title changed several times, but the thread connecting them never did.

That’s the real work of realignment: separating your transferable core from your job description. Most people skip this step because it means sitting with uncertainty, and that’s uncomfortable. It’s natural to want to replace what you’ve lost as quickly as possible just to feel stable again. But rushing can lead you right back into the same trap, tying your identity to a new title before you’ve figured out what truly fits.

I used to measure success by how far I advanced in one lane. Now I ask myself three questions before making any career decision, whether I’m choosing to pivot or being forced to change.

What here is mine, regardless of the title? Not the role, but the underlying capability: the thing I’d still be good at if the job disappeared tomorrow. For me, that was explaining complicated things simply. When I started food blogging, I thought of it as a complete departure from occupational therapy. Then I noticed the similarities. I was still educating, still communicating, still taking information and making it useful in people’s everyday lives. The setting and my title had changed, but the capability carried over, even outside a clinic.

Is this restlessness or fear? Restlessness is a signal that you’ve outgrown something. Fear of instability is also a signal, but a different one. Learning to tell them apart keeps you from staying stuck in roles that no longer fit.

What’s the smallest real test I can run this month? One conversation, one class, one small project, with no guarantee it will go anywhere. Clarity comes from small realignments, not from deciding everything in advance.

Today, I practice occupational therapy again, but differently, and on terms I chose rather than ones I inherited. Returning didn’t reverse my pivot. It was a realignment, because the constant was never the career. It was the values I carried through every change.

A title can disappear in a single day, but the capabilities underneath it rarely do. Anyone facing a career disruption can ask the same question: What would still be true about my skills, my values and the way I connect with others if my job were gone tomorrow? That answer is worth building toward long before a crisis forces the question. Purpose was never meant to fit inside one job description. It was meant to survive whichever one comes next.

I nearly passed out at work before I admitted something was wrong. It wasn’t that I didn’t recognize my symptoms were serious. It was that leaving my career felt more dangerous than the health problems I was struggling with.

That’s the part of the story I used to leave out, because it was the hardest to admit: My body was telling me to stop, and I kept ignoring it because I had built my whole identity around being unstoppable and around my role as an occupational therapist (OT). I had studied and trained extensively to become a licensed OT. I had formed close friendships with colleagues. I relied on the income. And I quietly believed that being an OT was what made me valuable. Eventually, my health declined further, and the decision I couldn’t make was made for me: I was forced to retire due to illness.

At first, I grieved what was. I felt anxious about the sudden change in our family’s finances, the disruption to our routines, and the loss of my identity without the title of “occupational therapist.” I expected those feelings. What I didn’t expect was relief.

#5488. A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 12:43 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 12:44 pm

Some startups dream of getting acquired by a big tech company. Suplari has now done it twice.

Docusign on Tuesday announced its acquisition of the AI-powered spending analysis company, five years after Microsoft bought the Seattle-based startup and nearly three years after the Redmond tech giant spun the company back out to its founders.

Financial terms of the latest deal weren’t disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari’s technology into its contract management platform, pairing the startup’s analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with Docusign’s Iris AI engine.

The idea is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms.

“Joining Docusign allows us to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company’s spending,” Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said in a statement.

It’s a remarkable double-dip in startup M&A for a company that was applying AI to corporate spending years before the current agentic boom.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh “Niki” Parekh, a Seattle tech veteran who previously held leadership roles at Trulia and Market Leader, along with Gerber, a longtime engineering leader, and product leader Brian White. Gerber and White had worked together at iConclude, an earlier startup that Gerber co-founded.

The startup, in its first incarnation, pulled together procurement and spending data scattered across corporate systems such as SAP, Workday and Oracle, and used machine learning to flag savings opportunities, supplier risks and other inefficiencies. The pitch was an alternative to having teams of analysts comb through the data in Excel or Tableau.

Gerber has traced the idea to his time at Apptio, the IT cost management company, where he helped lead machine learning work. That opened his eyes to the ways that connecting financial data with IT activity could turn up problems such as auto-renewing contracts and services still running for employees who had left.

By 2021, Suplari had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures.

Microsoft acquired Suplari in July 2021, saying it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The startup had about 40 employees at the time.

Then ChatGPT arrived in November 2022. Microsoft redirected all of its new-product investment to Copilot, Parekh recalled in a blog post earlier this year.

Succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers, “exactly the kind of investment Microsoft was now reserving for Copilot,” he wrote. By then, Suplari had become core to the finance and procurement operations of 40 to 50 of Microsoft’s most strategic customers.

“Microsoft concluded, and we agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again,” Parekh wrote.

Suplari’s founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft retaining a minority stake. Gerber, Suplari’s original CTO, led the spinout and became CEO. He had been chief AI strategy officer for Microsoft’s Dynamics finance and operations products after the acquisition.

Parekh stayed at Microsoft, working on Copilot Studio and the Power Platform, before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn.

Since the spinout, Suplari has added an AI agent that helps procurement teams act on what its software finds, Gerber said on an Art of Procurement podcast in June. Its customers include BT Group, Nordstrom and MediaNews Group, according to Docusign. The company has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Gerber declined an interview with GeekWire after the acquisition announcement, citing a quiet period. In a statement, Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari’s “technology and talent” will help Docusign connect what companies’ supplier agreements say with their actual spending.

Parekh has remained a Suplari shareholder and advisor. Asked about the deal, he said via email that generative AI is “enabling a renaissance in many ‘traditional’ systems of record” like enterprise resource planning and contract lifecycle management.

Connecting contracts with their outcomes, he said, “will be the future.”

As for Suplari’s own outcome, Parekh said he’s “ecstatic” about the startup’s second exit.

#5487. Why Didn't Bitcoin Drop More? Binance's CZ Credits FBI

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ) credited the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and other US law enforcement agencies with helping prevent a larger drop in the Bitcoin (BTC) price after the massive $6.3 billion security breach at the Binance cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance founder CZ commended the timely actions of the FBI, US Secret Service (USSS), and Internal Revenue Service (IRS) amid the massive security breach.

According to CZ's Nov. 1 post on X, US law enforcement agencies (FBI, USSS, IRS and more) helped "a lot" during the incident.

For instance, they helped with tracking and freezing funds.

According to the Binance co-founder, they were able to prevent an even sharper fall in the Bitcoin price.

"Not enough to express our appreciation in a tweet. There are probably a lot of crypto bros not realizing that a lot of 'why bitcoin didn't drop even more?' credits go to them," CZ stated.

This comes after the FBI officially identified North Korean hackers as being behind the record-breaking Binance hack.

According to the FBI's Oct. 31 announcement, North Korea stole more than $6 billion worth of cryptocurrencies from the Binance crypto exchange on or about Oct. 29.

More specifically, the FBI identified the North Korean cybercrime group TraderTraitor as being behind the massive cryptocurrency theft.

It's a known North Korean hacker group that has stolen large amounts of cryptocurrencies before.

The FBI noted that investigators, together with the Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation, have tracked how the hackers were exchanging stolen cryptocurrencies mainly for Ethereum (ETH).

The FBI warned that these assets could be further laundered using decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols and instant cryptocurrency swap services.

The US authorities have called on cryptocurrency businesses and infrastructure providers to block transactions related to the cryptocurrency addresses used by the hackers to stop them from laundering these assets.

Specifically, the US authorities urged THORNode operators, remote procedure call (RPC) node operators, instant exchanges, blockchain analytics companies, DeFi platforms, etc., to block such transactions.

Apart from that, the FBI provided a list of the cryptocurrency addresses used by the hackers to allow other members of the cryptocurrency industry to detect and block suspicious transactions.

The Binance security breach sent shock waves throughout the cryptocurrency market.

Bitcoin tumbled below $77,000 after the market reacted to the unprecedented crypto theft.

BTC dropped to around $76,000 at one point, registering its lowest price in several weeks.

Meanwhile, other major cryptocurrencies like Ethereum, XRP, Solana (SOL), and BNB nosedived as the market reacted to the breach.

Fortunately, Bitcoin eventually found stability and was trading around $78,000 during the early Nov. 1 trading session.

#5486. A year in, Smartsheet CEO Raj Singh bets on a new vision beyond the company’s flagship product

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 3:31 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:53 pm

Smartsheet’s biggest new product in years doesn’t require Smartsheet.

The Bellevue, Wash.-based company on Wednesday unveiled vsActual, as in “plan versus actual,” an AI product that reads a company’s strategy and budgets, tracks the work across tools such as Jira, Workday and Slack, and flags when projects drift off course.

It’s the first standalone product under CEO Raj Singh, the Concur co-founder who took over Smartsheet a year ago, and it’s aimed at CEOs, CFOs and COOs rather than the project managers who have long been Smartsheet’s core users.

At the company’s Engage conference in Seattle, Singh showed a slide from a year ago labeling Smartsheet “a product company,” with the company and its software in a single box.

“Smartsheet, the company, and Smartsheet, the product, were exactly the same thing — same box, same ceiling — an attractive ceiling, but still a ceiling,” he said. Now, he explained, Smartsheet is a multi-product company, with vsActual as a key milestone.

Singh was relaxed and at home on the stage, engaging warmly with the crowd and his fellow presenters like someone who’d been running Smartsheet for years. He went off script often enough that he paused at one point to reassure the teleprompter operator everything was OK, and his talk ultimately ran so long that it threw off the morning’s schedule.

In an interview with GeekWire after the keynote, Singh said the company has more room to grow by working with the software that customers already use than by trying to move everything into its flagship product.

“Most of the competition is saying, ‘Well, if you move all your stuff onto my platform, you’ll be totally in control,’” he said. “I think every CIO is thinking, I’m never going to do that.”

Founded two decades ago, Smartsheet is best known for spreadsheet-style software that teams use to plan projects, track tasks and automate routine work.

It went public in 2018 and was taken private in January 2025 by Vista Equity Partners and Blackstone in an $8.4 billion deal, when it had more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Its rivals include Microsoft, Google and Salesforce, as well as Asana, Monday.com, Airtable and ClickUp.

Singh described vsActual as part of a broader product lineup that also includes Smartsheet’s flagship software and Brandfolder, the digital asset management service the company acquired in 2020.

All three draw on the same underlying data, built from 20 years of tracking how work gets planned, approved and done in Smartsheet, which the company calls its Execution Graph. Future products will be built the same way, Singh said.

“The Execution Graph is the long-term differentiated value of our company,” he said.

A change in pricing: Smartsheet is also moving away from charging by the user. Under a new consumption-based model, customers pay a base fee plus credits that are drawn down as people use the software, including its AI features, automations and API connections. Seat-based plans remain available.

Singh said customers balked at paying full price for people who use Smartsheet only occasionally. As an example, he said creating a dashboard might cost 50 cents, rather than a license that runs hundreds of dollars. Customers who switch won’t be charged for going over their credits, though he didn’t say for how long.

He said the net effect on revenue should be “nothing but positive,” describing the shift as a way to unlock demand from customers who held back under per-seat pricing.

“Agents are clearly going to be users moving forward,” he added.

Competition and risks: The new product enters a crowded field. Microsoft, ServiceNow, Workday and others are adding AI agents that plan and track work inside their own products, and AI-native startups are going after the same status-report busywork.

The software also depends on data from systems run by other companies, including rivals such as Asana. Singh said Smartsheet connects to them through APIs and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for linking AI models to outside software, depending on how deep the integration goes.

The approach carries some risk: if companies can track their work through vsActual without moving it into Smartsheet, they have less reason to expand their use of the core software, the company’s main business.

Asked about that, Singh pointed to new AI features in Smartsheet itself, including its Smart Assist agent and an MCP server that lets customers use Smartsheet from AI assistants such as Claude and Copilot. “The core keeps growing,” he said.

Keith Kirkpatrick, a Futurum Group analyst, wrote Wednesday that vsActual is “the company’s clearest move yet from managing tasks to governing strategy,” but said the strategy requires Smartsheet to sell to a different kind of buyer.

“Its sellers are also not used to finance-led deals with long evaluation cycles,” he wrote, adding that many executives still see Smartsheet as a “glorified Excel” project management tool.

Singh said Smartsheet’s sales force already knows how to sell to large enterprises, but acknowledged that the company will need people who understand corporate planning. It will build a team of vsActual specialists, as it has for Brandfolder.

Kirkpatrick also noted that vsActual requires a company to work from one official plan, unlike Smartsheet’s more flexible core software, and said the company will need to show that its Execution Graph offers the same depth for customers whose work lives mostly in other systems.

“Decoupling widens the market but strains the main differentiator,” he wrote.

Smartsheet hasn’t said when vsActual will be generally available or how it will be priced. It’s building the product with 12 enterprise design partners, including some of the world’s largest food service, financial services and health systems, Singh said.

From Concur to Smartsheet: Singh started Concur in the early 1990s with his brother, Steve Singh, and Mike Hilton, and the company grew into a top provider of corporate travel and expense software before SAP acquired it for $8.3 billion in 2014.

Raj Singh later led health benefits company Accolade through its IPO and sale, and took over as Smartsheet CEO in October 2025, after longtime CEO Mark Mader retired and Apptio co-founder Sunny Gupta served as acting CEO.

Smartsheet cut jobs that month and again in February. Singh has since rebuilt the leadership team, including several executives he worked with at Concur and Accolade.

Singh said the leadership team is now fully assembled and the company is hiring, though AI means headcount won’t grow the way it once did.

He didn’t disclose revenue but said the business is growing, especially internationally and with government customers, and that retention remains strong despite fears that AI would lead companies to abandon traditional software. More than 100 customers now pay Smartsheet at least $1 million a year, a record, he said.

He credited Smartsheet’s founders and past leaders with building a successful tool for project managers, calling former CEO Mark Mader and co-founder Brent Frei friends.

Singh said the bigger opportunity is to help businesses run better, and he sees no reason Smartsheet can’t become one of the most important software companies in the world.

“I’m 58 years old,” he said. “I’m not doing this because I need to make an extra buck. I’m doing this because I think there’s a very important company in here, and we just have to unearth it, and then we have to get to customers and make them see that new vision.”

#5485. 1.8 Billion XRP Moves in Just 24 Hours as XRP Ledger Shows Signs of Recovery

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

A headline claiming that 1.8 billion XRP moved across the XRP Ledger within 24 hours has revived discussion of a network recovery. The figure hasn't been independently verified for a dated 24-hour period, so treat it as a reported claim, not confirmed evidence of a new trend.

The XRP Ledger handles payments, decentralized exchange transactions and tokenized assets. Payment volumes reflects the network activity, but the number needs context. Large transfers can be exchange custody movements, internal treasury operations or transfers between wallets controlled by the same entity.

None of that necessarily signals fresh investor demand or new capital entering the market.

Recent verified reporting shows why the distinction matters. One October snapshot had daily payment volume jumping to about 137.7 million XRP, still below its 30-day average of roughly 496 million.

Another October reading, around 363.3 million XRP, came with the same caution: a one-day rise did not establish a sustained recovery.

A reading near 1.8 billion XRP usually comes at the end of the week where most of the network activity occurs. The most likely outcome is always the same: high activity by Thursday and Friday and a tubmling on the weekend, with a recovery starting on Monday.

Other indicators help separate real adoption from a passing spike: active addresses, successful payment counts, decentralized-exchange trading, liquidity and how transaction sizes are distributed. Even high transaction counts can mislead when automated activity dominates, as recent investigations into small-value stablecoin payments on XRPL showed.

Network usage and XRP's market price are only indirectly related. More settlement activity doesn't guarantee higher token prices, and speculative buying can lift prices with no matching improvement in usage. Broader market conditions and exchange liquidity matter too.

A verified natural burst of XRP movement could mean renewed engagement with the network. A more convincing signal would be several consecutive days of stronger, widely distributed activity, backed by improving liquidity and sustained user demand, which rarely happens.

#5484. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5483. Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 5:41 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:54 pm

People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”

Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”

It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.

For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.

The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.
